Security researchers at pwn.ai demonstrated that simply viewing a crafted email in Roundcube could trigger remote code execution without clicking the attachment. Similar attacks were successfully tested against Debian 13 print servers, WordPress, Forminator, Elementor, and other applications under specific configurations.  The vulnerability, dubbed Upload2Shell, carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and affects Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader. Attackers can disguise malicious PostScript files as ordinary images or documents, exploit a memory corruption flaw, bypass Ghostscript's -dSAFER sandbox, and execute commands with the permissions of the affected service.  Researchers also identified vulnerable processing paths involving MediaWiki, DokuWiki, Plesk, and several document management systems. The attacks exploit how applications pass untrusted files to Ghostscript through image conversion and preview functions.  Artifex patched the underlying vulnerability in Ghostscript 10.08.0, released September 8, with additional fixes issued by affected software vendors and Linux distributions. Administrators are urged to install patched versions and verify that applications and containers are not using vulnerable Ghostscript builds. Propagation: Automated spread to up to 50 contacts per day via contextually aware malicious messages.  The listing offers the exploit chain in three tiers: a Single Target License for $8,000, an Operator License for $15,000 (up to 50 devices), and an Enterprise License for $45,000 (unlimited deployment). Deliverables purportedly include full source code, pre-compiled binaries for Android ARM64/x86_64 and iOS ARM64, C2 infrastructure code, and a 150-page technical manual. The actor claims the exploit has not been disclosed to vendors and no CVE has been assigned.  The threat actor behind this listing has a limited public history, with previous posts on other platforms appearing to be automated rendering probes or low-signal activity rather than confirmed high-profile breaches. There is no independent evidence linking this actor to major past incidents. At the time of reporting, the existence of this specific zero-day exploit, the claimed FUD status, and the validity of the stolen carrier certificates have not been independently verified. Security researchers have not publicly corroborated the specific technical details provided in the forum post.

The threat actor claims to possess extensive membership records containing sensitive personal and financial information, including credit card details, IBANs, account balances, email addresses, and phone numbers, reportedly affecting more than two million members.  According to the listing, the allegedly compromised data spans multiple database tables containing personal, financial, and identity-related records. The actor provides the following breakdown of the claimed data volume:  VA011_SOG_ALL (Member Registry): 2,042,243 rows VA011_SOG_ALL joined with deposit and balance tables: 2,193,549 rows ESTRAZIONE_VOTANTI_2023 (Voter Extraction): 1,099,928 rows TA013_DOC_SOG (Identity Documents): 492,207 rows TP002_DEP (Deposit Accounts): 460,242 rows TP036_SAL_DEP_ANN (2026 Balances): 224,512 rows IL_SALESFORCE_BACKUP (Contact Block): 108,174 rows TP104_IBN (IBANs): 18,324 rows  The forum listing also includes purported data samples containing Italian tax identification codes (Codice Fiscale), dates of birth, residential addresses, and bank account information with associated balances.  Unicoop Firenze published a statement regarding the data leak situation on November 17, addressing the incident through its official communication channels.  If the threat actor's claims are substantiated, the exposure of personal and financial records could create significant risks for affected members, including targeted phishing campaigns, identity theft, and financial fraud.  The threat actor's history on underground forums appears limited, with no clearly established track record of major data breaches. The authenticity and full scope of the allegedly compromised dataset have not been independently verified.

After Hugging Face there was this silly discourse about how you can't do anything against zero-day exploits.  Assume you have one of those enterprise gateway/firewall appliances that have zero-days found in their web management interfaces every other week.  For arguments sake, I'm going to simply accept that you can't take the management interface offline. You can't configure it to be accessible only from the local network. It has to be accessible to anyone connecting from anywhere.  The overwhelming majority of threat actors (including state-sponsored ones) tend to be overly reliant on internet scanning. They use services like Shodan/Censys, which scan every IPv4 address, then create indexes listing all the devices they find.  Threat actors then come along, use a search query to export a list of "<insert appliance type> by <insert vendor>", then either mass-exploit them, or pick and choose the devices belonging to organizations they're interested in.  One option: Create a subdomain, ideally something not easily guessable like "firewall-​a4f8d5.​yourcompany​.com".   Sign up for a proxy/CDN provider like Cloudflare or similar. Configure the provider to forward traffic designated for that domain to the public IP address of your appliance, then enable revere proxy mode.  Now, go into your firewall and set up a rule to block all access to the management interface from IPs not belonging to Cloudflare. Either with an CIDR or ASN allow list.  Your device now doesn't show up in any internet scans at all, including those provided by Shodan or Censys, and the device is not directly accessible via IP address. But it is still accessible to anyone with the domain.  You've now reduced your blast radius from "every zero-day (or n-day if you don't patch immediately) is rocking my device" to "99.9% of exploitation attempts don't even see it", all without sacrificing availability.  Highly targeted attacker may go to the extra effort of figuring out the subdomain you use, and try to exploit the devices through the reverse proxy. But the way reverse proxies work breaks a lot of exploits, and Web Application Firewalls add a layer of additional protection.  Techniques like this work for most web-based appliances (which tend to get hit a lot as the result of internet scans). And there are plenty of simple things you can do for other software/devices which massively reduces your attack surface. Just one extra layer between the attacker and the target works wonders.  The whole "zero-day exploits are unstoppable" attitude is extremely defeatists, and also extremely wrong. Ask your friendly neighborhood blue teamer or threat intelligence professional for attack surface reduction advice.

I have so many theories as to why this is.   1) A learned helplessness in the rank and file, instituted over the past two decades by a bipartisan leadership style that dictated to members in a top down manner what they were going to do and enforced it punitively using campaign cash, committee seats, etc, as leverage.   2) At least on the R side, we have reached a critical mass of senators who have never seen a functioning Senate. They have no idea how powerful they actually are or how the Senate operated in the Before Times (not even that long ago! Like in the 90s and early 2000s!).  Current senators either don’t want to know and outsource that knowledge to staff who are disinclined to do anything with it, or are gaslit into believing they require permission to use their considerable privileges. (The latter point drives me absolutely bananas. What’s the point of being a senator if you have to ask Mother May I every single time you want to BE A SENATOR. No wonder they’re all leaving for different jobs.)  3) The Senate has completely atrophied as a problem solving institution. Usually when things get stuck there are bipartisan “gangs” that form to solve the issue, lead negotiations, or walk the Senate back from the brink. This doesn’t happen anymore largely because senators don’t feel they have individual agency. See points 1 and 2.   4) Also per the last point, the committees are too large, and senators are on too many, to allow them to focus on two or three things and become The Guy about That Thing.   5) The committees are also deferential to leadership in a way they didn’t used to be, and that lack of independence dulls vital skill sets because it relies on other people to chew your food for you.  6) The modern Senate will do nothing unless they have a predetermined outcome. How many times has “we don’t have 60” been used as an excuse to do nothing? The Senate is a majestic institution precisely BECAUSE it is designed to leverage uncertainty into consensus. You never know how things will actually end until you fight them to the floor and give issues a political process, force a negotiation, and don’t give up until you’ve come to a solution. The greatest causes in American history didn’t *begin* with 60 or 67 (former cloture threshold) votes. They ended there after massive exertion and process. Modern Senates refuse to countenance a) the workload required and b) the uncertainty of the outcome.   (more below)
